macOS app updates

Foreground and background signed app updates from standard GateFox GitHub releases.

About 6 min read · 3 sections

On this page
01 Release tags and names 02 Release availability 03 Desktop verification limits

The installed app checks for app releases when it opens or becomes active, and every five minutes while active. Repeated foreground events within five minutes share the previous check. The existing background service also checks daily. It uses the GitHub CLI's existing login to read GateFox releases; the updater never asks for, stores, or prints a token. A release provides one notarized app ZIP, its matching gateway backend archive, app-update.json, and SHA256SUMS.

An update notice appears above every app page, with Install Update, and the sidebar shows Update available. After staging, Quit & Finish Update closes the control panel through its normal cleanup; running chats continue. Failed checks are visible with Check Again, instead of silently hiding update status. Settings retains manual checks and the automatic-install preference. The existing signed updater handles downloads and activation; no separate updater job or Sparkle dependency is added. A CLI-only release or prerelease does not announce an app update: the full signed app release must be published.

Release tags and names

Current app releases use vVERSION and count as updates only when they carry app-update.json and its complete asset set. A command-line-only release is ignored.

Tag App ZIP (app inside) Backend archive
vVERSION GateFox-VERSION-macos-arm64.zip (GateFox.app) gatefox-VERSION-macos-arm64.tar.gz

A set is accepted only whole: a GateFox ZIP must hold GateFox.app and its archive must unpack to gatefox-VERSION-macos-arm64. Historical app-vVERSION tags and Harness Gateway asset names remain recognised for existing installations and recovery. They are not the publication format for new releases. The rules live in src/app-updates/names.ts.

Renaming the installed app to GateFox.app

An updater swaps a release into the app's existing path. If that path is still Harness Gateway.app, at its next launch the app renames itself to GateFox.app in the same folder, leaves Harness Gateway.app as a link to it, and relaunches from there (AppRelocation.swift). The link is required: launchd keeps the loaded job's old program path until the next login, and the service plan stores the old app's Node path for the Claude components, so without it the service cannot restart and those components fail until then. The new instance's usual background association then moves the service plist's Program and the install's app-runtime link to the new path. Both accept the old path as the previous owner only when it is the Harness Gateway.app beside the running GateFox.app (src/app-bundle.ts); any other path is still refused. The bundle identifier and signature do not change, so macOS permissions stay.

The rename is skipped while GateFox.app already exists, while an update journal (app-update-transaction.json) exists, or while app-update.json records a pending update, because those record the old path. It happens at a later launch instead. If the relaunch fails, the app moves back and keeps running. The service keeps running throughout; the new Program applies at its next start.

GitHub draft → signed ZIP + signed policy → update check
                                               ↓
                                    checksum and receipt validation
                                               ↓
                             wait for every app window to close
                                               ↓
                           activate retained bundle / preserve CLI service

The updater downloads both the matching canonical CLI archive and signed app ZIP. It checks their hashes, app metadata, and signed in-bundle update-policy.json before activation. The policy binds the app to the exact backend archive version, production commit, and SHA-256. It refuses missing, partial, modified, or mismatched assets.

Activation waits until every app window has closed. It preserves active chats and jobs: processes already loaded from the earlier CLI release continue, then adopt the installed CLI release through their normal idle-update protocol. Opening the app before an update is ready keeps the current bundle active.

The updater retains the previous app bundle for transaction rollback. A failed installation transaction restores that retained bundle; it does not claim to detect or roll back a later launch failure. The gateway configuration remains unchanged.

After a successful installation is acknowledged and its transaction journal is finalized, the updater removes that update's downloaded ZIP, backend archive and extracted staging files. It only cleans the exact owned app-update-<uuid> folder whose manifest, archive digest and tree match the completed update. Pending, foreign, changed, linked or in-use installation paths are never guessed at. The retained rollback app bundle and installed current/previous releases stay. Cleanup failure does not undo or misreport an otherwise successful update.

Recovery restores only files that still match the transaction's publication receipts. It preserves concurrent changes. A forced termination can leave an unknown installation lock, which the updater will not break automatically. After confirming that no installer or updater remains, move only the stale .gateway-installation-lock directory in the installation root to Trash before retrying.

Update transactions skip the installer's release pruning, so the same cleanup then runs after the update is finalized (src/app-updates/retention.ts). It keeps the current and previous releases, the newest other release, and any release a running process or saved service plan refers to. It also removes gateway generations beyond the newest 12 that are at least three days old and unreferenced. Both come back from a release download or the next engine start. An incomplete inventory, or a process running through current whose source release cannot be identified, prevents all of this; so does an open update transaction.

The CLI installer bounds each process/open-file inventory at 64 MiB so busy Macs can complete the release-retention check. A timeout, overflow or incomplete scan still prevents pruning; it never establishes that an old release is unused.

Release availability

The updater sees an app release only after its draft assets have all uploaded, their GitHub-reported sizes and SHA-256 digests match local files, and the draft is published. The current updater uses the GitHub CLI's saved login for release discovery and downloads. Configure that login as a deployment prerequisite; the app does not provide a separate GitHub sign-in flow.

Use the local production release command described in Release. It does not dispatch, enable, or rerun GitHub Actions. Follow the CI cost policy: hosted native work stays off unless Edi explicitly requests its separate paid, production-only workflow. Before the release is uploaded, that command runs the updater fixture against an existing signed app and installed CLI release in a fresh private fixture directory; no live service is changed.

Desktop verification limits

The October 18 inspection found one gateway startup job on Studio and MacBook. MacBook's Login Items panel still displayed two enabled GateFox rows. Reading the records behind those rows required administrator authorization, so their exact cause remains unverified. No background-item reset or service restart was used to clear the display.

Existing services keep their loaded runtime until their normal idle upgrade. Matching signing requirements and passing isolated runtime checks do not prove that a macOS privacy grant survives an app update. That check still needs an existing approved action on an unlocked Mac; no privacy grants were reset or automatically accepted during verification.
